row.title: Why thirteen?
statutory_hooks: RSHE 2026 (online safety and awareness, the minimum age for social media)
RSHE 2026 (wellbeing online, why services are age restricted)
KCSIE 2026 para 165 commerce (online gambling, inappropriate advertising)
row.evidence_anchor: The minimum age of 13 on social media comes from data protection law, not from a judgement about maturity: under the UK GDPR, 13 is the age at which a child can consent to their own data being processed
row.single_action_outcome: I can say what the number on an app is protecting.
row.character_cast: Bloop opens with the shield, DiGi closes on choosing on purpose

slides.title: Why thirteen?
slides.body: Every app asks how old you are. Today you find out what it does with the answer.
slides.script: Settle everyone with this slide up. Read the title, then the line under it, then stop. Do not open by asking who has an account, and do not open with a warning. Some of this class already has accounts and the lesson only works if that stays completely ordinary. Today is not about catching anybody out. It is about finding out what a number actually does.

slides.heading: Bloop has a question
lines: Every app I open asks me when I was born.
I always thought it was being nosy.
Turns out it is building me a shield. Let us find out how.
slides.script: Let Bloop land the frame before you say anything. The shield is the tool for today and it arrives here, in the character's mouth, so the class meets it as an idea rather than as a rule. Bloop already carried the privacy shield in the lesson on what not to share, so say that out loud if your class did that one: same friend, same shield, new switch.

slides.outcome: I can say what the number on an app is protecting.
slides.why: You will be asked your age by every app you ever open. Knowing what the answer does is more use than being told a rule.
gains: What the number 13 actually means, and where it comes from
The four things an app switches on when it believes you are a child
Why games and gambling sites carry numbers too, and what they are for
slides.script: Read the outcome and the why slowly. Then name what today is not, because half the room is expecting it: this is not a lesson telling anybody they are not allowed. It is a lesson about what a number does, and by the end they will know more about it than most adults do. That is a genuinely fair thing to promise and it changes how the hour is received.

slides.prompt: An app asks for your birthday before it will let you in. Why do you think it wants to know?
slides.lookFor: Most say to check you are old enough. Some say to send birthday messages. Listen for the child who says so it knows what to show you, because that is the whole lesson and it is the most useful answer in the room.
slides.script: Ninety seconds in pairs, timer on screen. Take three answers and do not judge any of them. If anyone says so it knows what to show you, write it up, because you are coming back to it in five minutes. If nobody says it, that is fine, you will hand it to them instead.

slides.heading: Three words for today

words.meaning: A number on an app, a game or a website saying who it was built for. It is not a guess. Somebody chose it, for a reason.
Something switched on to keep you safer. The best ones work quietly, so you never notice they are there.
Everything the app switches on when it believes you are a child. Your age is what holds the shield up.

slides.script: Say each word, class repeats it. Spend your time on shield, because the other two are nearly self explanatory and shield is the one doing the work today. Hold your hand up flat as you say it. That gesture comes back three times this lesson and the children will start doing it with you.

slides.heading: Every app asks your birthday
slides.body: Before an app lets you in, almost all of them ask when you were born. It is not being nosy and it is not really about birthdays. That one answer decides what kind of person the app thinks you are, and everything it does next is built on it.
slides.script: This is the hinge of the lesson, so slow down. The key idea is that the birthday question is not a formality, it is the first and biggest decision the app makes about you. Say the last sentence twice. Everything it does next is built on it.

slides.question: An app asks Maya for her birthday. What is the app actually trying to find out?

options.text: Whether to send her a birthday message
options.feedback: Some do that, but it is not why they ask. The real answer is bigger and it is about what she is shown.

options.text: Whether she is a child, so it knows which rules to run
options.feedback: Exactly right. The app is sorting her into child or adult, and those two get completely different versions of the same app.

options.text: Nothing, it just likes forms
options.feedback: It would be easier for the app to skip the question. It asks because the answer changes what it does.

slides.script: Hands or devices. The first option is the popular wrong answer because birthday messages are a real thing, so give that feedback warmly. Land the second one hard: the app is sorting people into two groups and the two groups get different apps.

slides.heading: Thirteen is a real rule, not a guess
slides.body: Nearly every social media app says you must be at least thirteen. That number is not somebody's opinion about when children are ready. It comes from a law about your information: thirteen is the age the law says you can agree to a company collecting and using your data. Under that, a company is not allowed to take it without a grown up saying yes.
slides.script: This is the fact most adults in the building do not know, so deliver it as a fact and not as a warning. Thirteen is a data protection age, not a maturity age. Two things follow and both are worth saying. One, the rule is about a company's behaviour and not about whether a particular child is sensible. Two, that is exactly why the rule does not bend for being mature for your age. It was never measuring that.

slides.prompt: If an app believed you were twenty five, what might it start showing you that it would not show a ten year old?
slides.lookFor: Scary things, rude things, adverts, strangers messaging. All good. Steer gently away from naming specific content and towards the categories, which is where the learning is.
slides.script: Sixty seconds, whole class, hands up. Take four answers and sort them out loud into the four the next slide names: what you see, who can reach you, what is sold to you, and what happens if you ask for help. You are building the diagram with them rather than presenting it at them. Keep it brisk and do not let it become a competition to name the worst thing.

slides.heading: The shield has four parts
slides.caption: All four are switched on by one answer: the age the app believes you are.

steps.title: What you see
steps.text: Filters run harder. Frightening, rude and grown up content is held back before it ever reaches you.

steps.title: Who can reach you
steps.text: Adults you do not follow cannot message you, and your account is harder for strangers to find.

steps.title: What is sold to you
steps.text: Adverts are limited, and the app is not allowed to build a full profile of you to sell to advertisers.

steps.title: What happens if you ask for help
steps.text: If you report something, the help tools know a child is asking. That changes how fast and how carefully it is handled.

slides.script: Walk the four steadily, pointing at each. The fourth is the one to dwell on, because it is the one nobody expects and it is the most important: if the app thinks you are an adult, then when you ask for help, an adult is what asks. Land the verdict chips at the end. One answer, four protections, and every one of them works quietly, which is exactly why they are so easy to throw away.

slides.heading: The protections are wired to the number
slides.body: Here is the part worth remembering for years. Those four things are not switched on because the app likes you. They are wired to the number you typed. Change the number and they all let go at once. Nobody announces it. The app looks exactly the same, and the shield is simply not there any more.
slides.script: Deliver this one flatly and let it sit. The word wired is doing the work: it means automatic, it means all four together, and it means nobody checks afterwards. The silence is the dangerous part. Nothing on the screen tells you the shield has gone, which is why this has to be taught rather than discovered.

slides.question: Which one of these is the app actually looking at when it decides what to show you?

options.text: How sensible you seem in your messages
options.feedback: It cannot see that. It has never read a single thing about who you are as a person.

options.text: The number in the birthday box
options.feedback: That is all it has. One number, and four protections hanging off it.

options.text: How long you have had the account
options.feedback: Makes no difference. A brand new account with a real birthday has the whole shield up.

slides.script: Quick one, thirty seconds. This is the cycle two check and it exists to make one idea stick: the app has a number and nothing else. If pupils are still answering as though the app can tell what kind of person they are, that is the thing to correct before you move on to games.

slides.text:
Enter your date of birth

Day  01   Month  01   Year  ▾

(scroll for more years)
slides.script: Put this up and say nothing for five seconds. Then ask one question: how long would it take to scroll that year up by ten? The answer is about two seconds, and that is the whole point of the slide. The easiest thing on the screen is the thing that switches off all four protections, and nothing about the box tells you that.

slides.question: Sam scrolls the year up so the app thinks he is nineteen. What happens to the four protections?

options.text: They stay on, because he is still the same person
options.feedback: The app cannot see him. It can only see the number, and the number now says nineteen. All four let go together.

options.text: All four switch off, and nothing on the screen says so
options.feedback: That is it exactly. The app looks identical. The filters relaxed, strangers can reach him, his data is fair game, and if he reports something the help tools think an adult is asking.

options.text: Only the adverts change
options.feedback: Adverts change, but so does everything else. The number is one switch holding all four, which is why it matters so much more than it looks.

slides.script: Whole class. Watch for pupils choosing the first option, because it is the kind hearted answer and the reasoning behind it is good: he IS the same person. Say that out loud before you correct it. He is the same person and the app cannot see people, only numbers. That distinction is the lesson.

slides.heading: The rule is not a judgement about you
slides.body: This is worth being clear about, because age rules can feel like being told you are not good enough. They are not about that. Nobody has measured you. The number is a rule about what a company is allowed to do with a child's information and a child's attention, and it applies to every single person your age in the country, including the sensible ones. That is what makes it a protection instead of an insult.
slides.script: This slide exists because the honest objection from a bright ten year old is but I would be fine. Answer it properly rather than dismissing it. The rule is not a measurement of them, it is a limit on a company, and limits on companies do not have exceptions for impressive children. Delivered this way, most of the room stops arguing, because you have agreed with the true part of what they were about to say.

slides.heading: Games carry numbers too
slides.body: It is not only social media. Games carry an age number on the box or the store page, usually a 3, 7, 12, 16 or 18. That number is not about how hard the game is. It is a warning about what is inside it: how frightening it is, how violent it is, whether strangers can talk to you while you play, and whether it will keep asking you for money.
slides.script: Most of this class thinks a game rating is a difficulty rating, and that misconception is worth killing directly. Say the four things the number is actually warning about and count them on your fingers. The one they will not expect is whether strangers can talk to you, so pause there. A game can be perfectly gentle and still carry a high number because of who else is in it.

slides.question: A game says 18 on the store page. Priya says it is fine because the game is easy. Is she right?

options.text: Yes, if it is easy it must be suitable
options.feedback: The number was never about how hard it is. An easy game can still be full of frightening things, or full of strangers who can talk to you.

options.text: No, the number is about what is in it and who is in it, not how hard it is
options.feedback: Exactly. Difficulty and age rating are two completely different things, and mixing them up is the most common mistake there is.

options.text: It depends whether her friends play it
options.feedback: How many friends play it changes nothing about what is inside it. That is a reason it feels fine, not a reason it is fine.

slides.script: This is the misconception check for the whole cycle, so take it seriously. The third option is the social pressure trap and some children will pick it honestly. Use its feedback out loud and do not mock anyone: everyone plays it is a real feeling and a bad reason, and saying both halves is what makes the correction stick.

slides.heading: Three kinds of number, three different jobs
slides.caption: Different rules, one habit: before you sign up, find the number and ask what it is for.

steps.title: Social apps
steps.text: Usually thirteen. It is about your information and who is allowed to reach you.

steps.title: Games
steps.text: 3, 7, 12, 16 or 18. It is about what is inside, and who else is inside with you.

steps.title: Gambling sites
steps.text: Eighteen, and this one is the law rather than a company's rule. Betting is not allowed for children at all, and sites that ignore that are breaking the law.

slides.script: Walk the three. The third needs the clearest voice: gambling is the one where the number is the actual law rather than a company setting, and where the answer for a child is simply no rather than not yet. Do not moralise, just be factual. Then land the three verdict chips as the habit the whole lesson is building.

slides.heading: The ones that are really about money
slides.body: Some things carry an eighteen because of what they do to people rather than what they show them. Gambling is the clearest one: paying money for a random chance, designed by experts so that the machine wins in the long run. Some games borrow the same trick with prize boxes you pay to open. Knowing the trick is the defence, and you already know it.
slides.script: If your class did the gaming and spending lesson, point straight back at it, because they met the loot box there and this is the same machine wearing a different hat. If they have not done it, one sentence is enough: paying for a random chance is how gambling works, and it is built so the machine wins. Do not extend this into a lesson about gambling. Today it is one of three kinds of number.

slides.prompt: Why do you think apps make the birthday box so easy to scroll, when the answer matters that much?
slides.lookFor: The honest answer is that more users is better for the company. Some children get there on their own and it is a genuinely sharp thing to notice. Others will say the app cannot check, which is also true and worth having.
slides.script: Sixty seconds in pairs. This is the most grown up question in the lesson and some classes land it beautifully. Both true answers are worth having: the company benefits from more users, and the company genuinely cannot check. Say the second one carefully, because the takeaway is not that nobody is watching, it is that the only person who can protect the shield is the person typing.

config.heading: Half time · everyone together
config.prompt: Two breaths: in as Bloop grows, out as Bloop shrinks. Then tell your neighbour one thing from today that surprised you, and write it on your sheet.

slides.script: Half time. Two breaths with the whole room, in as Bloop grows and out as Bloop shrinks. Then thirty seconds in pairs on one thing that surprised them, and they write it on their sheet. Nothing is marked and nobody reads theirs out. This lesson runs on one idea repeated, which is tiring in a different way from a busy lesson, so the pause earns its place here. Then straight into the sorting task.

slides.caption: Age spotters

items.text: A drawing app with no chat and no account
items.why: Nothing to sign up to, nobody to talk to, nothing being collected. Fine.

items.text: A game rated 12 when you are nine, with voice chat on
items.why: Two reasons rather than one: the number is above you, and the voice chat means strangers are in the room with you.

items.text: A social app your cousin says everyone is on, minimum age 13
items.why: Everyone is on it changes nothing about what switches off. The number is thirteen and thirteen is what it is.

items.text: A homework site your school asked you to use
items.why: Chosen by your school, for your age, for a reason. Fine.

items.text: A game rated 7, but it keeps asking you to buy prize boxes
items.why: The age is fine and the spending is not automatically fine. That is exactly the kind of thing to check with a grown up first.

items.text: A site that lets you bet on football scores
items.why: Eighteen, and this one is the law rather than a setting. Not yet is the only answer.

slides.script: Five minutes. Read each card, class votes with fingers for one, two or three, then reveal. The third card is the one to slow down on, because everyone is on it is the pressure this lesson is actually arming them against. The fifth card is deliberately not a clean no: the age is fine and the money is the problem, and noticing that two different things are being judged is the point.

slides.heading: The shield sheet, on paper
slides.body: Pick one app or game you use. Write down what you think its number is, then write one sentence saying what that number is protecting.
slides.script: Five minutes on the sheet from the pack. They do not need the number to be right, and say so before they start, because half of them will not know it and will stall. Guessing the number and explaining what it is for is the whole exercise. Circulate and collect one good sentence to read out at the end.

slides.prompt: Swap sheets. Read your partner's sentence. Does the protection they named match the kind of app they picked?
slides.lookFor: A social app should get something about who can reach them or what is collected. A game should get something about what is inside it. A mismatch is a good conversation rather than a mistake.
slides.script: Sixty seconds. This is peer marking without calling it that, and mismatches are the useful outcome rather than the failure. Take two examples, one match and one mismatch, and talk the mismatch through warmly.

slides.question: Which of these would actually switch the shield on for a ten year old?

options.text: Typing your real birthday when it asks
options.feedback: Yes, and it is almost the only thing on this list that does anything. The true answer is what holds the shield up.

options.text: Choosing a strong password
options.feedback: A good idea for a different reason. It protects your account from being broken into, but it does not switch any of the four protections on.

options.text: Only using it at weekends
options.feedback: That is about how much, not about what. The shield is the same on a Saturday as on a Tuesday.

slides.script: The two wrong answers are both genuinely good habits, which is what makes this question work. Say that clearly as you give the feedback: these are not silly answers, they are right answers to different questions. Today's question is what holds the shield up, and there is only one answer to that.

slides.question: Exit check. What is the number thirteen on a social app actually about?

options.text: Whether a company is allowed to collect and use your information
options.feedback: Correct, and it is the answer most adults get wrong. It comes from a law about data, not from anybody's opinion about maturity.

options.text: Whether you are sensible enough to cope
options.feedback: That is what it feels like and it is not what it is. Nobody measured you. It is a limit on what a company may do.

options.text: How many friends you need before you join
options.feedback: Nothing to do with friends. It is about your information and who is allowed to reach you.

slides.script: Ten seconds of quiet thinking, then vote. If a large part of the room picks the second option, that is worth knowing and worth one more sentence before you move on, because it means the insult reading is still winning over the protection reading.

slides.question: Exit check. Why does typing a fake age matter more than it looks?

options.text: Because four protections are wired to it, and they all let go at once without telling you
options.feedback: That is the sentence to take home. Nothing on the screen changes. The shield is just gone.

options.text: Because you would get in trouble for lying
options.feedback: Getting in trouble is not the risk here and this lesson is not a telling off. The risk is that the protections quietly stop.

options.text: Because the app would stop working properly
options.feedback: It works perfectly. That is exactly the problem: it looks identical, and the shield is not there.

slides.script: Same routine. The second option is the answer a child gives when they think the adult wants a rule followed, so use its feedback out loud and mean it. This lesson is not a telling off, and saying so one more time on the way out is worth doing.

slides.heading: What to remember
points: Every app asks your age because the answer decides which version of the app you get.
Thirteen comes from a law about your information, not from an opinion about you.
Four protections are wired to that number: what you see, who can reach you, what is sold to you, and what happens when you ask for help.
Games carry numbers about what is inside them and who is inside with them, not about how hard they are.
Find the number, ask what it is for, then choose. That is the whole habit.
slides.script: Read the five points at a steady pace and let the last one land as the takeaway. Find the number, ask what it is for, then choose. That sentence is what you want them repeating at the door, and it is a habit rather than a rule, which is the difference this whole scheme is built on.

slides.heading: Bloop's mission for you
lines: Tonight, find the number on one app you use.
It is usually in the app store, right near the download button.
Then tell somebody at home what that number is protecting. Shield up!
slides.script: Let Bloop give the mission, the bubbles appear on their own. The mission is deliberately findable: the age is genuinely on the store page and takes about ten seconds, so this is a mission most of them will actually complete, which is the point.

config.heading: The passport
config.prompt: Today filled a little of the Social media ready page. Tap to fill it in.
config.after: A full page brings the big check, and the big check earns Bloop's stamp.

slides.script: The passport page fills as the class taps. This one lands on the social media ready area, which is the right home for it: the judgement is being built years before any account exists, which is exactly what the area is for.

slides.heading: DiGi closes the mission
lines: You know something now that a lot of grown ups do not.
That number was never about whether you are good enough.
It is a shield. And now you know what it is made of. See you next lesson!
slides.script: Let DiGi land the ending, the bubbles appear on their own. Exit quizzes go out as this plays, named copies from the print room. Collect them on the way out.

exit_quiz.instructions: Four questions on today. Keep this in your book.

in_lesson_checks: The choice on what the app is really asking, after the first concept
The choice on what happens to the four protections, after the birthday box
The choice on the easy 18 rated game, which is the misconception check for the whole cycle

action_commitment.stem: Tonight I will find the number on ______, and tell ______ what it is protecting.
action_commitment.note: Collected on the learning record. The app is theirs to choose and the person at home is theirs to choose, which is what makes it get done.

teacher_judgement.secure: Can say that the age decides which version of the app you get, and can name at least two of the four protections without prompting.
teacher_judgement.developing: Knows the number matters and describes it as a rule about being allowed rather than as a protection that switches things on.
teacher_judgement.needs_support: Reads the age rule as a judgement about them personally, or as a rule that can be earned by being sensible.

parent_note.headline: What we taught today, and one thing to try at home
parent_note.taught: Today your child learned what the age number on an app or a game actually does. The short version: it is not a judgement about whether they are sensible. Thirteen on social media comes from a law about data, and when an app believes it is talking to a child it switches on four protections, covering what they see, who can reach them, what is advertised to them, and how a report for help is handled. Change the age and all four let go at once, silently.
parent_note.try_this: Ask them to show you the age number on one app they use. It is on the store page, right next to the download button, and it takes about ten seconds to find. Then ask them what they think that number is protecting. They will be able to tell you, and most adults cannot.
parent_note.family_question: What is that number for? Then: what would switch off if the app thought you were twenty five?
parent_note.passport: This lesson filled part of your child's passport page. The passport is the readiness record home and school build on the road to sixteen: skills proven at school, trust earned at home, each stage stamped when it is ready rather than when a birthday arrives. The skill proven today is being able to say what an age rule is protecting.

teacher_notes.learning_objective: To explain what an age rule on an app, a game or a site is protecting, and what changes when the age is wrong.
teacher_notes.timing: 63 minutes: starter 9, cycle one 10, cycle two 10, cycle three 10, practise 15, prove 4, close 5

cycles.title: Every app asks your birthday
cycles.outcome: I can say what an app is really asking when it wants my age.

cycles.title: The protections are wired to the number
cycles.outcome: I can name what switches off when the age is wrong, and that nothing on screen says so.

cycles.title: Games carry numbers too
cycles.outcome: I can tell the difference between an age rule about content, about contact, and about money.

teacher_notes.tool: SHIELD: find the number, ask what it is protecting, then choose.
prior_knowledge: Builds directly on the privacy lesson, where Bloop introduced the shield for what not to share, and on the gaming lesson, where the class met paying for a random chance. Neither is required. If your class has done them, name them out loud, because the continuity does real work here.
key_learning_points: The age answer sorts a user into child or adult, and the two get different versions of the same app.
Thirteen is a data protection age, not a maturity age, which is why it does not bend for a sensible child.
Four protections are wired to the age: content filtering, who can make contact, advertising and profiling, and how a report is handled.
Nothing on screen changes when they switch off, which is why this must be taught rather than noticed.
Game ratings describe content and contact, not difficulty. Gambling at eighteen is law rather than a company setting.
misconceptions: That an age rating measures difficulty. This is the most common one in the room and the third cycle exists to kill it.
That the age rule is a judgement about whether this particular child is sensible. Answer the true part of the objection first: they may well be fine, and the rule was never measuring that.
That lying about your age is wrong mainly because lying is wrong. The lesson deliberately does not run on that, because a child who only hears do not lie learns nothing about what was lost.
i_can: I can say what the number on an app is protecting.
teacher_notes.commitment_stem: Tonight I will find the number on ______, and tell ______ what it is protecting.
teacher_notes.teacher_tip: Some children in the room already have accounts they are too young for, and some of their parents set them up. Nothing in this lesson requires anybody to admit that and nothing in it blames a family. Teach the mechanism, not the compliance. If a child says they have one, a neutral good to know and a move on is the right response in front of the class, and a quiet word afterwards if anything concerns you.
teacher_notes.equipment: Projector. The shield sheet from the printed pack, one per child. No pupil devices needed.
teacher_notes.paper_fallback: The whole lesson runs from the printed pack with no screen: the four protections are a diagram on the pack, the sorting cards are on the back page, and the birthday box is described in the run sheet for you to read aloud.

differentiation.support: focus on two of the four protections rather than all four, and use the hand up flat gesture as the memory hook.
differentiation.stretch: ask why a company might prefer people to get the age wrong, which is the sharpest question in the lesson and some Year 6 pupils will reach it unaided.

teacher_notes.send: The four protections are named with one picture each and can be taught as four pictures without the text. The shield gesture gives a non verbal route into the recall. Pre teach shield with a physical object if that helps, and keep the birthday box slide up for longer than the script suggests, because the scrolling year is the whole idea in one image.

evidence_base.claim: Thirteen is the age at which a child can consent to their own data being processed by an online service in the UK, which is where the minimum age in most social media terms of service comes from.
evidence_base.source: UK GDPR, age of consent for information society services
evidence_base.status: Stated in the lesson as a legal fact about data, not as a readiness threshold.

evidence_base.claim: Game age ratings describe content, contact and spending features rather than difficulty.
evidence_base.source: PEGI rating system, used across the UK
evidence_base.status: The third cycle is built on this, because the difficulty misconception is the most common one in the room.

evidence_base.claim: Gambling has a statutory minimum age of eighteen in the UK, which is law rather than a platform setting.
evidence_base.status: Taught as the one age rule on the slide where the answer for a child is no rather than not yet.

hard_questions.question: But my mum set mine up.
hard_questions.answer: Parents can and do, and nothing today says your mum was wrong. What you know now is what the number was protecting, and that is worth knowing either way. If you want to, you can ask her to check the age on the account with you.

hard_questions.question: What if I am already on it?
hard_questions.answer: Nothing in this lesson asks anybody to delete anything. The useful move is to check the age on the account with a grown up at home, because it can usually be corrected, and correcting it switches the protections back on.

hard_questions.question: Why does nobody check?
hard_questions.answer: Because the app genuinely cannot see you. It only has the number. That is not a reason to relax about it, it is the reason the only person who can hold the shield up is the person typing.

hard_questions.question: I would be fine though.
hard_questions.answer: You might well be. The rule was never measuring you. It is a limit on what a company is allowed to do with any child's information, and limits on companies do not have exceptions for impressive children.

parent_questions.question: Are you telling my child they cannot use anything?
parent_questions.answer: No. The lesson explains what a number protects and gives them the reason behind it. What your family allows is your decision, and the lesson is written not to cut across it.

parent_questions.question: Will this make my child feel guilty about an account we set up?
parent_questions.answer: It is written specifically to avoid that. Staff are told not to treat an existing account as a confession, to meet it neutrally in front of the class, and to follow anything concerning up quietly afterwards.

parent_questions.question: Is thirteen really a safety age?
parent_questions.answer: It is a data protection age. We say so in the lesson. The safety part is the four protections that sit behind it, and those are what your child can now name.

subject_knowledge.heading: Where thirteen actually comes from
subject_knowledge.body: Thirteen appears in most terms of service because of data protection law rather than developmental research. Under the UK GDPR, thirteen is the age at which a child can give their own consent to an information society service processing their data; below it, a parent must consent. It is not a maturity threshold and no study establishes it as one. That is why the lesson frames it as a rule about what a company may do, and why it does not bend for a sensible child. If a parent or a pupil pushes on this, the honest answer is that the number is a legal line about data, and the protections that sit behind it are the part that matters.

subject_knowledge.heading: Three kinds of age rule, deliberately taught apart
subject_knowledge.body: Social media minimums come from data law. Game ratings in the UK come from PEGI and describe content and, increasingly, contact and spending features rather than difficulty. Gambling carries a statutory minimum of eighteen, which is law rather than a company setting. Teaching these as three different kinds of rule rather than as one big rule about being old enough is what makes the knowledge portable to apps that do not exist yet, which is the whole point of teaching a mechanism.

subject_knowledge.heading: Why the lesson does not run on do not lie
subject_knowledge.body: A child who only hears that lying about an age is wrong has learned nothing about what was lost. The four protections are the content, and the deceit is not the subject. This also keeps the lesson usable in a room where some children have accounts their parents set up, which is most rooms. Teach the mechanism, not the compliance.

dsl_note.note: This lesson is about a mechanism rather than about harm, and carries no disclosure prompt. Two things to watch for anyway. A child may reveal an account they are too young for, which is not in itself a safeguarding concern and should be met neutrally in front of the class. A child may describe contact from an adult on a platform, which is, and should go to the DSL the same day under your safeguarding policy. The teacher tip tells staff to take anything concerning quietly afterwards rather than in front of the room.
